title: How I test UI/UX, animation, and motion-heavy websites
excerpt: A general QA guide for visual polish, responsive behavior, scroll animation, 3D sections, reduced motion, and cross-browser checks.
author: Kiran Dhakal

sections.title: Start with the user journey, not the animation library
paragraphs: A polished website can still fail if motion hides important content, interrupts reading, or behaves differently across devices. I start UI/UX testing by identifying the goal of each page: what the user must read, click, understand, or trust.
For a motion-heavy site like an interactive company website, I would test scroll speed, keyboard navigation, touch gestures, resize behavior, and content visibility before judging visual effects.

sections.title: What I check in animation QA
items: Text does not overlap during entrance, exit, hover, or scroll states.
Animated sections remain usable when the user scrolls quickly.
3D or canvas content loads, frames correctly, and has fallback behavior.
Reduced-motion settings still allow the user to reach all content.
Animation does not block buttons, forms, navigation, or focus states.

sections.title: Responsive and cross-browser coverage
paragraphs: I compare mobile, tablet, laptop, and wide desktop layouts. On each viewport I check spacing, readable font sizes, touch target size, image cropping, sticky headers, and footer behavior.
Cross-browser checks should include Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge when possible. The evidence should name the browser, device size, scroll position, and exact visual problem.

sections.title: Release evidence
paragraphs: For UI/UX QA, useful release evidence includes screenshots, short videos, viewport dimensions, browser versions, performance notes, and reduced-motion observations. A vague report like 'animation broken' is weak; a report with timing, screen size, and expected behavior is actionable.
